item.text: I’m reproducing the C++ program as a standalone Rust project in `/output`, but I’m treating the underlying color operation as a black box and will infer it from the compiled binary rather than reading the C++ library sources. First I’m probing the executable’s behavior across inputs so the Rust output matches exactly.

The sample output already matches a simple saturation model around the channel average. I’m checking edge cases now to confirm whether the implementation clamps, how it handles negative factors, and whether formatting follows ordinary `std::cout` defaults or needs a custom formatter.

I’ve narrowed the color operation down to HSL saturation scaling, not a simple distance-from-average transform. Next I’m matching the exact float behavior and output formatting, because the C++ binary already shows a small rounding artifact on an extreme case.

item.text: The HSL model is right, but a few random probes differ in the last printed digit. That usually means the library is doing the math in `double`-like precision and only rounding back to `float` at the end, so I’m checking that variant before I write the final files.

Those last-digit mismatches were from my probe harness, not the algorithm: I was feeding the C++ binary rounded CLI strings but evaluating the Rust side on the original in-memory floats. I’m rerunning the comparison with both sides using the same parsed argument strings, which is the actual behavior of the program.

I’m using the compiled binary as the reference, but I’m also compiling a tiny standalone C++ probe with a few plausible HSL implementations. That lets me identify the exact precision/cast pattern without ever reading the original library source.
